Paper Title: Democratizing science with the aid of parametric design and additive manufacturing: Design and fabrication of a versatile and low-cost optical instrument for scattering measurement
Parametric Methods: Parametric design was implemented using Grasshopper (visual programming for Rhinoceros 3D) and custom parameter-driven geometry-generation algorithms controlling shape, tolerances, and infill; a component-specific algorithm governs support base, base cylinder, inner cylinder and pipe holder generation [1].
Am Technologies: Additive manufacturing used FDM desktop 3D printing (MakerBot II) with thermoplastics (PLA and tested ABS and Carbon-reinforced PLA); slicing/software workflow used CuraEngine/Repetier and GCode-based printers [1].
Customization Approach: Customization is achieved by exposing geometry parameters in Grasshopper (profile shapes, radii, heights, tolerances, infill, etc.), a sequential algorithm that recalculates on parameter change, and modular reusable blocks allowing mixing standard off-the-shelf parts (PVC pipes, electronics) with custom printed parts [1].
Key Findings: Key findings: parametric design + AM enable minimized tolerances and press-fit assembly, material and time savings through tailored infill and geometry (20-80% infill/material savings reported), modular, low-cost functional instrument demonstrated as proof-of-concept [1].
Application Domain: Primary application: scientific instrumentation / optical measurement (experimental physics). Authors also suggest broader applicability across low-cost instruments and OSAT contexts [1].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability is addressed via modular component design, parameter-driven re-scaling and profile substitution (virtually limitless designs), printable-size constraints awareness, and pre-print estimates of time/cost to support scalable production decisions [1].

Paper Title: Optimization Methodology for Additive Manufacturing of Customized Parts by Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Application to a Shoe Heel
Parametric Methods: The paper uses visual programming parametric design implemented in Grasshopper, combined with Python scripting for custom computations and scripts (e.g., Gh Python) [2]. The workflow defines parametric variables for heel geometry (multiple design variables controlling shape, curvature, support surface and offsets) and constructs the initial parametric volume in four subsections to enable automated variation and optimization [2].
Am Technologies: The study targets Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) using ABS filament and configures manufacturing constraints (minimum bar diameters, printing direction considerations, tolerances) to suit FDM processes [2].
Customization Approach: Customization is achieved by feeding user-specific data (scanned foot geometry and gait analysis) into a parametric model whose parameters (heel position along waist curve, curvature, support offset, infill cell size, shell scale factor, etc.) are varied and optimized in a continuous workflow, producing individualized optimized geometries and lattice structures [2].
Key Findings: The paper demonstrates a continuous methodology that integrates topology optimization, lattice/infill design and size optimization to produce a variable-density cellular heel tailored to user data; key results include a manufacturable FDM-compatible topology-optimized heel with optimized infill and wireframe shell, variable bar diameters driven by local stresses, and a Pareto-based multi-objective optimization workflow yielding trade-offs between volume and structural stress [2].
Application Domain: Product design with a biomechanical/ergonomic focus (footwear — shoe heel); authors also suggest applicability to medical/biomechanical devices and other structural parts or furniture [2].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are addressed by a continuous parametric-dataflow that allows automatic generation and multi-objective optimization of many design variants (e.g., Octopus-driven evolutionary optimization yielding populations and Pareto fronts). Design variables (infill cell size, heel advance, width offsets, shell scale) are bounded to manufacturing limits so the workflow can produce many manufacturable variants suitable for mass customization [2].

Paper Title: Integration of Additive Manufacturing, Parametric Design, and Optimization of Parts Obtained by Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). A Methodological Approach
Parametric Methods: Parametric design is implemented through Grasshopper (visual/graphical programming) integrated with Rhinoceros; generative/algorithmic modeling, parametric variables, visual programming nodes and plug-ins (e.g., Millipede, Karamba, Octopus mentioned as compatible) are central to the approach [3].
Am Technologies: Primary AM technologies discussed and used for validation are FDM (focused in case studies) and SLS (tested); general discussion of layer-by-layer additive manufacturing and infill/shell concepts are included [3].
Customization Approach: Customization/personalization is achieved by parameterizing designs within a continuous Grasshopper workflow (variables control initial volume, infill, shell, load/support locations), producing variant solutions without remodelling; supports mass customization contexts especially with FDM [3].
Key Findings: Key findings: presents a methodology integrating additive manufacturing, parametric design (Grasshopper) and optimization (topology, size, multi-objective) in a continuous workflow; demonstrates variable-density infill and wireframe shell optimization producing lightweight, manufacturable parts; method supports mass customization and is validated on FDM case studies [3].
Application Domain: Application domains: product design and small-prototype manufacturing (validated on FDM), suggested applicability to medical devices/orthoses, fashion, ergonomics and construction contexts where customized lightweight parts are relevant [3].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability/variation: enables rapid generation of variants via parametric variables (no remodelling) and supports multi-objective optimization (Octopus) to explore Pareto fronts; proposes continuous and hierarchical workflows to manage computational complexity and decompose problems for higher-detail or alternative designs—facilitating scalability from coarse to fine levels and many variants [3].

Paper Title: Design Automation for Mass Customisation via Additive Manufacture: A Case Study on Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Mask
Parametric Methods: Parametric design approach using a large-scale statistical shape model learnt from 9,663 facial scans [12], with an automated pipeline that generates CAD from a single facial image [12].
Am Technologies: Additive Manufacturing (AM) generally discussed as the production technology enabling one-off/custom items; specific AM processes or machines are not mentioned in the provided text [12].
Customization Approach: Customization achieved via an automated parametric pipeline that uses a single facial image to generate a patient-specific CPAP mask CAD model rapidly, removing manual CAD steps and simplifying data acquisition [12].
Key Findings: Demonstrated a fully automated parametric pipeline for creating patient-specific CPAP mask CAD models from a single photograph, trained on a large statistical shape model of 9,663 scans; achieved rapid CAD generation (<1 minute), significant reduction in design time and removal of manual modelling, and proposed transferability of the workflow to other wearables to promote AM adoption for mass customization [12].
Application Domain: Medical devices / wearables (case study on CPAP mask) [12].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability enabled by AM's low tooling cost for one-off items and by automated design pipeline which reduces per-item design cost and time, allowing broader adoption and potential application to other wearables [12].

Paper Title: Product customization and generative design

Am Technologies: Discusses additive manufacturing/3D printing as the enabling fabrication technology, including selective laser sintering and 3D-printed soles/garments and complex lattice/internal mesh fabrication enabled by AM [13].

Application Domain: Application domains include automotive, aerospace, architecture, footwear, jewellery, and apparel (product design and architecture) [13].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are addressed through algorithmic generation of large numbers of design iterations and immediate parametric feedback enabling rapid variant generation and selection; examples cite tens of thousands of iterations versus manual dozens [13].

Paper Title: PARAMETRIC MODELING OF BIO-INSPIRED LUMINAIRES FOR ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING TECHNOLOGIES

Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation addressed via parameter-driven variation in parametric models enabling easy modification of geometry [14]; manufacturing constraints (nozzle size, layer height) are considered and leveraged (e.g., vase mode in FGF) to scale detail vs production speed and to process different materials, supporting variation and production trade-offs [14].

Paper Title: An interactive product customization framework for freeform shapes

Key Findings: The prototype was validated across four example applications (hollow patterned bicycle helmet; T-rex with skin frame structure; face mask with Voronoi patterns; AM-specific night dress with hollow patterns), demonstrating the system's ability to produce varied freeform, AM-tailored designs, and the prototype is publicly available [15].

Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are addressed through AM's capacity to fabricate complex geometries without tooling, and by supporting user-driven parametric edits of styling curves to generate multiple design variants; explicit scalability analyses are not mentioned in source [15].

Paper Title: An additive manufacturing process model for product family design
Am Technologies: The study uses Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) as the primary AM technology, mentioning it as a layer-by-layer extrusion process [16]. A Panowin F321 FDM printer was used in the case study [16], and Polylactic Acid (PLA) was the feedstock material [16].
Customization Approach: Customization is achieved by using topology optimization to generate optimal, variant-specific geometries for each product variant, exploiting AM's ability to fabricate complex, tool-free parts [16]. The model evaluates many designs and selects suitable ones based on combined performance and cost metrics [16], with final realization via FDM fabrication [16].
Key Findings: The model can enable affordable customization by integrating topology optimization, FEA and cost modeling to select product family designs; physical fabrication and testing validated the approach [16]. It increases customization compared to traditional product family methods by exploiting AM capabilities while balancing cost and performance [16]. FEA predictions matched experimental deflections within expected material property bounds [16].
Application Domain: Product design / mechanical components (case study on cantilever beams) [16].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability is addressed by defining a 'scalable product family' where platform parameters (dimensions/material fraction) are varied to generate a continuum of variants; the model evaluates an effectively infinite design space via topology optimization and interpolates performance and cost to select designs, enabling variation and scaled customization [16].

Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are addressed by using simplified models and parametric optimization loops for iterative exploration, and by integrating AM constraints to minimize material and printing time, enabling production of multiple unique panels efficiently [17].

Paper Title: Parametric design and adaptive sizing of lattice structures for 3d additive manufacturing
Parametric Methods: Parametric geometric parameterization using bounding-box dimensions, aspect ratios, and thickness to define lattice unit-cell geometry; analytical automation with a rigidity model using 3D beam elements for adaptive sizing and mechanical parameter adjustment [18].
Am Technologies: 3D additive manufacturing (general 3D printing) with reference to material extrusion (MEX) benchmark lattices (cross, hexagonal) and use of FEM validation tools (ANSYS Mechanical) for manufacturability and structural analysis [18].
Customization Approach: Customization via fully parameterized lattice unit cells: adjusting bounding-box dimensions, aspect ratios and thickness to tailor geometry to load states and constraints, coupled with analytical/numerical (FEM) validation and manufacturability simulations to ensure printable, support-free designs [18].
Key Findings: Proposed pyramidal lattice achieves superior structural efficiency (better mass-to-displacement ratio) compared to cross and hexagonal lattices; analytical rigidity model validated by FEM shows consistent structural predictions; design is manufacturable without supports in 3D printing simulations [18].
Application Domain: Industrial design engineering / product components (plastic parts) for additive manufacturing applications [18].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability via parametric definition and superposition: unit-cell parameterization allows scaling and tiling into matrices; analytical rigidity models enable evaluation of larger assemblies and adaptation to varying load/boundary conditions [18].

Paper Title: Additive manufacturing and its effect on sustainable design
Parametric Methods: The chapter references parametric modeling and parametric design representations (3D CAD models and parametric modeling methods) as part of the AM design workflow; specific tools (e.g., Grasshopper) are not named in the text [24].
Am Technologies: Discusses the full ASTM F2792 taxonomy of AM technologies: material extrusion (FDM), powder bed fusion (SLS, SLM, DMLS, EBM), vat photopolymerization (SLA), material/binder jetting, sheet lamination (LOM), and directed energy deposition; the chapter also discusses specific systems (e.g., Fortus 450mc) and process details [24].
Customization Approach: Customization/personalization is achieved via digital CAD/STL workflows and on-demand printing (print-on-demand), enabling one-off or short-run bespoke parts without tooling; the chapter emphasizes designer-maker workflows and distributed manufacturing as mechanisms for user-specific adaptation [24].
Key Findings: Findings: AM enables sustainability opportunities (material efficiency, lightweighting, part consolidation), supports extensive customization and distributed on-demand production, and enables new DFAM/DFP methods (topology optimization, lattice/cellular design). However, the authors call for more quantitative research and lifecycle-integrated design methods; they propose a sustainable DFAM methodology and show a case study (triple clamp) demonstrating reduced parts count and lower environmental impacts [24].
Application Domain: Application domains covered include aerospace, automotive, biomedical, consumer products, jewellery, furniture, designer-maker/craft contexts, and an applied case study in motorcycle components (triple clamp) [24].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are addressed via digital parametric/voxel-based modeling enabling high degrees of design freedom, topology optimization and lattice/cellular structures for lightweighting, part consolidation to reduce part counts, and distributed on-demand manufacturing to scale production geographically; the chapter also discusses limitations (energy, support material, post-processing) and need for lifecycle-aware optimization [24].

Paper Title: A Cost-Driven Design Methodology for Additive Manufactured Variable Platforms in Product Families
Am Technologies: Not mentioned in source.

Key Findings: A fuzzy time-driven activity-based costing method (FTDABC) with ANFIS is used to estimate AM production costs based on process settings [25]; the feasible space boundary for process adjustments is found via multi-objective optimization [25]; case studies show optimized variable platforms improve performance at lower cost than consistent platform-based designs [25].
Application Domain: Product design (consumer product: R/C racing car family) [25]
Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are managed by constraining design and process adjustments within a bounded feasible space to limit cost increments [25], and by computing platform parameter limits via an expert system used as optimization constraints to support scalable variation while optimizing customer utility [25].

Paper Title: Cloud-Based Automated Design and Additive Manufacturing: A Usage Data-Enabled Paradigm Shift
Parametric Methods: The paper discusses parametric design models and highly parametric/root-design approaches for automated adaptation of designs, including storing design parameter values for variant generation and extending parametric design to include local material properties [26].
Am Technologies: AM is central: the paper names AM process classes (material extrusion, material jetting, powder bed fusion, directed energy deposition, binder jetting, sheet lamination, vat photopolymerization) and highlights directed energy deposition and multi-material approaches for sensor integration and local property control [26].
Customization Approach: Customization/personalization is achieved via a Usage Data-Enhanced Cloud-based Design and Manufacturing (UDE-CBDM) workflow: products collect usage/PEID data into a cloud repository; a DaaS (Design-as-a-Service) tool uses root-design parametrization and usage data to adapt parameter values and generate individualized variants; AM fabricates variants, enabling tailor-made production and mass-customization [26].
Key Findings: Key findings: authors propose the UDE-CBDM paradigm combining usage-data, cloud services (DaaS), parametric/automated design, and AM; AM enables item-level customization and sensor integration but technical gaps remain (no single AM process for full 3D sensor integration, multi-material challenges, software/toolchain gaps); many enabling components exist yet integration, certification, privacy/security, and virtual testing remain open research needs [26].
Application Domain: Application domains covered: medical implants (patient-specific implants/prosthetics), robotics (robot components and closed-loop adaptive systems), and consumer products (athletic shoes/mass-customization); also broader mentions of tools, tooling, spare parts, and IoT-enabled products [26].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation: the paper situates AM in Conner et al.'s regions, highlighting AM's role in mass-customization (Region VI) and discusses storing parameter sets for scalable variant generation; cloud infrastructure and multi-agent systems are proposed to scale data processing and distributed manufacturing, but current MAS prototypes and AM production rates present scalability limits that require development [26].

Paper Title: Customized Design for Ergonomic Products via Additive Manufacturing Considering Joint Biomechanics

Paper Title: User Driven Custom Design - the solution to simplify customisation according to consumer needs

Customization Approach: Customization is achieved via a user-facing web configuration platform allowing selection and direct customization of wheelchair components (frame, accessories, cushion, footrest), combined with parametric modelling driven by anthropometric and behavioural data and a recommendation engine to map user inputs to product specifications [29].
Key Findings: The approach enables customer-driven customization while reducing time, cost, material waste, and unnecessary machining through anthropometry-driven parametric design; it demonstrates replication and scale-up potential in medical applications [29].
Application Domain: Medical devices (wheelchairs) as the primary case study, with suggested applicability to fashion, furniture, and sports equipment [29].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability is discussed in terms of replication and scale-up potential in medical domain and enabling mass customization via AM for accessories and tools; specifics on production scale or process scaling are not provided [29].

Paper Title: Parametric Topology Optimization Toward Rational Design and Efficient Prefabrication for Additive Manufacturing
Parametric Methods: The paper uses parametric level-set based topology optimization methods, specifically a distance-regularized parametric level set approach [30].
Am Technologies: Stereolithography (SLA) additive manufacturing is the primary AM technology discussed; the framework outputs mask images directly usable in the AM process [30].
Customization Approach: Customization is enabled through topology optimization that can produce multiscale and multimaterial structures, supporting mass customization by creating designs with high geometric complexity [30].
Key Findings: The framework reduces prefabrication computational cost by integrating parametric topology optimization with SLA-aware outputs and a prefabrication-friendly procedure, verified by simulation and experiments showing significant cost reduction without sacrificing design intent or functionality [30].
Application Domain: Product/structural design domain demonstrated via test examples: a free-form 3D cantilever beam and a multiscale meta-structure [30].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability and variation are addressed by generating multiscale and multimaterial structures and by reducing prefabrication numerical complexity to make production of complex or mass-customized variants computationally feasible [30].

Paper Title: Mathematical pattern for parametric design: the case study of Grey-Scott cross diffusion model

Paper Title: MASS CUSTOMIZATION : REUSE OF TOPOLOGY INFORMATION TO ACCELERATE SLICING PROCESS FOR ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING

Paper Title: DETC 2018-85645 CUSTOMIZATION OF A 3 D PRINTED PROSTHETIC FINGER USING PARAMETRIC MODELING

Customization Approach: Customization is achieved by parameterizing finger geometry based on measured anthropometrics (finger length and width) from 50 participants and generating prosthetic finger variants from those parameters rather than using uniform scaling; parametric designs better match natural ROM [109].

Application Domain: Medical devices / prosthetics (upper limb prosthetic fingers) [109].
Scalability Aspects: Scalability/variation is addressed by parameterizing geometry to generate variants across the measured anthropometric range (tested with highest and lowest length-to-width ratios from 50 participants) and fabricating via AM; contrasts with uniform scaling approach [109].

Key Findings: La tesis destaca: (1) las ventajas geométricas y de proceso de la fabricación aditiva (obtener geometría final en un único proceso) [111], (2) la libertad geométrica permite optimizar diseños con mayor complejidad y más soluciones factibles [111], y (3) la metodología propuesta fue validada mediante un estudio de caso [111].

Scalability Aspects: Escalabilidad/variación: la metodología soporta mayor complejidad geométrica y multiplica las soluciones factibles, y emplea rellenos parametrizados que varían a lo largo de la pieza para responder a diferentes solicitaciones mecánicas, lo que facilita adaptación y variación en escala y función [111].
